source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC4803651 (journal version; J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2016;77(2):185-198), read in full in the built-in browser: abstract, methods, results, Tables 1-5, discussion, limitations, conclusions, funding footnote. Figures 3 and 4 checked on screen (their values are printed in the figures). Online Appendices A-F (study list, codebook, funnel plot, covariate table, covariate-removal details, heterogeneity of the higher-quality studies) not read.

claims.note: Only the magnitude cites this source. Every Stockwell 2016 number in it matches Tables 2 and 3: limited adjustment 0.95 (0.91-1.00), 1.12 (1.07-1.17), 1.29 (1.22-1.36); all covariates 1.07 (0.97-1.18), 1.24 (1.12-1.37), 1.44 (1.30-1.60). The reference group is 'abstainers' as each study defined them, and 74 of 87 studies put former and/or occasional drinkers in it. The full model adjusts for those abstainer biases at study level, so 'against non-drinkers (study level)' is right. The pooled models agree with the statement that death rates rise from about 45 g a day. One qualification: in the strictest subsets, against lifetime abstainers only, the 45 to under 65 g group was not clearly raised (13 studies 1.11, 0.93-1.32; 7 studies 0.95, 0.62-1.46; 6 studies 1.07, 0.83-1.36). In the 6 higher-quality studies, 25 to under 45 g was raised (1.29, 1.06-1.56). With limited adjustment, 25 to under 45 g was slightly lower than abstainers (0.95, p = .031). Those subsets are small, so they do not overturn 'close to no difference' at 25 to 44 g, but they show the threshold is not well defined in bias-free studies. The limitations paragraph supports the caveat that self-reported intake is mostly under-reported. Intake was measured once, at baseline, as mean daily grams. Recomputed (editors' arithmetic, not from this source): 45 g x 7 = 315 g a week; 25 g x 7 = 175 g a week; 100 g a week / 7 = 14.3 g a day. All correct.

anchors.locator: Table 2; Results › Synthesis of results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality with limited adjustment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Limited adjustment (precision and between-study variation only), 87 studies, 523 estimates, against abstainers as each study defined them, by mean g ethanol a day at baseline. Medium 25 to under 45 g: RR 0.95 (95% CI 0.91-1.00), p = .031, 63 studies. High 45 to under 65 g: 1.12 (1.07-1.17), 44 studies. Higher 65 g or more: 1.29 (1.22-1.36), 33 studies. I2 79.5%, 82.0% and 83.3%. No significant Egger test.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (both panels and footnotes); Results › Synthesis of results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality after adjustment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Six covariates (median age at intake, sex, Caucasian or not, adequacy of the drinking measure, former-drinker bias, occasional-drinker bias): medium 0.98 (0.92-1.04), high 1.13 (1.06-1.20), higher 1.32 (1.23-1.41). All identified covariates (adding years of follow-up, exclusion of ill participants, and study-level control for race and smoking): medium 1.07 (0.97-1.18, p = .17), high 1.24 (1.12-1.37), higher 1.44 (1.30-1.60). Former and high-volume drinkers were significantly raised in every model.

anchors.locator: Table 4 Model 4; Table 5 Models 1 and 2; Results › Synthesis of results › Meta-analysis of higher quality studies, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Against strictly defined lifetime abstainers: 13 bias-free studies (adjusted for median age, sex and country): medium 0.95 (0.80-1.13), high 1.11 (0.93-1.32), higher 1.42 (1.15-1.75). 7 higher-quality studies: medium 1.08 (0.72-1.62), high 0.95 (0.62-1.46), higher 1.58 (1.05-2.38). The same without the influential Friesema 2007 (6 studies): medium 1.29 (1.06-1.56), high 1.07 (0.83-1.36), higher 1.85 (1.51-2.27). In these subsets the 45 to under 65 g group is not significantly raised, and the 25 to under 45 g group is raised in the 6-study model.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph; Method › Data items › Measures of alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exposure was mean daily grams of ethanol assessed at baseline. The authors note that self-reported consumption is mostly under-reported and that even the classification as lifetime abstainer can be unreliable.

claims.note: Every Stockwell 2016 number in the statement and magnitude matches the source: 87 studies; 3,998,626 people; 367,103 deaths; low volume 1.30-24.9 g a day; 0.86 (0.83-0.90); occasional 0.84 (0.79-0.89); former 1.22 (1.14-1.31); against occasional drinkers, low volume 1.02 (0.95-1.10) and abstainers 1.19 (1.12-1.27); six covariates 0.89 (0.84-0.94); all covariates 0.97 (0.88-1.07) with former 1.38 (1.24-1.54); 13 bias-free studies 0.90 (0.76-1.06) with former 1.31 (1.09-1.57); 7 higher-quality studies 0.89 (0.62-1.29), and 1.04 (0.95-1.15) without Friesema. 'Most studies included former or occasional drinkers' is right: 74 of 87 did (65 former, 50 occasional, 41 both). 'Mostly North America, Europe and Australia' is right: 77 of 87. The definitions are the paper's own: occasional is up to one drink a week (under 1.30 g a day); low volume is up to two drinks (1.30-24.9 g a day). The 1.30 g a day boundary is 9.1 g a week, about one 10-g drink (recomputed). 'Some of them because of illness' is the authors' explanation ('likely' because people quit for health reasons), not a finding of this paper. Small points: only 81 of the 87 studies contributed low-volume estimates, and the 2014 search limit means this source covers studies to 2014, not 2021. Qualifications the claim does not state: (1) In the stratified models (Table 4), the point estimate in bias-free studies (0.90) is about the same as in studies with both abstainer biases (0.91, 0.83-1.00). The bias-free result loses significance mainly because its interval is wider. (2) In Figure 3, removing the abstainer-bias covariates moved the adjusted estimate only from 0.97 to 0.96. The larger shifts came with removing study-level smoking control (0.91) and all covariates (0.86). So in this paper the attenuation is not driven mainly by how non-drinkers were defined, although the authors say an online appendix (not read) confirms the importance of former-drinker bias. (3) In the 7-study model including Friesema, former drinkers were not significantly raised (1.14, 0.77-1.69). The statement's 'in the main models (1.22 to 1.38)' holds for Tables 2 and 3. The claim does not overstate. Its 'insufficient evidence' wording is more careful than the paper's abstract, which says low-volume drinking has 'no net mortality benefit'. The adjusted interval (0.88-1.07) still allows a 12% reduction.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Method; Results › Study selection, 1st paragraph; Results › Study characteristics including controls for potential bias, 1st paragraph; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 87 prospective cohort studies of all-cause mortality (English-language, to 31 December 2014), 3,998,626 people, 367,103 deaths, 523 risk estimates. 77 of 87 studies (88.5%) from North America, Europe or Australia; 10 from Japan, China or India. Median of study median ages 54.5 years. Mean follow-up 13.4 years. Reference-group coding: 41 studies with both former and occasional drinkers among abstainers, 24 with former only, 9 with occasional only, 13 (127 estimates) with lifetime abstainers only.

anchors.locator: Method › Data items › Measures of alcohol consumption, 3rd paragraph; Method › Analyses, 4th paragraph; Method › Quality assessment, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Categories in mean g a day at baseline: occasional, up to one drink a week (under 1.30 g); low volume, up to two drinks (1.30-24.9 g), chosen from the Australian 20 g guideline and set at 24 g because people report whole drinks; medium 25-44.9; high 45-64.9; higher 65 or more. Lifetime abstention was coded strictly as zero lifetime drinking. Abstainers in week or month usual-pattern measures were assumed to include occasional drinkers.

anchors.locator: Table 2; Results › Synthesis of results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality with limited adjustment, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Limited adjustment, against abstainers as each study defined them: low volume 0.86 (0.83-0.90; 81 studies, 229 estimates; I2 65.0%), occasional 0.84 (0.79-0.89; 15 studies), former 1.22 (1.14-1.31; 21 studies). With occasional drinkers as the reference: abstainers 1.19 (1.12-1.27), low volume 1.02 (0.95-1.10, p = .52), former 1.45 (1.33-1.59). I2 above 50% in every category; no significant Egger test.

anchors.locator: Table 3; Results › Synthesis of results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality after adjustment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Six covariates, including former- and occasional-drinker bias: low volume 0.89 (0.84-0.94), occasional 0.86 (0.80-0.92), former 1.26 (1.17-1.35). All covariates (adding follow-up years, exclusion of ill participants, study-level race and smoking control): low volume 0.97 (0.88-1.07, p = .59), occasional 0.95 (0.85-1.05), former 1.38 (1.24-1.54).

anchors.locator: Figure 3 (values printed in the figure); Results › Synthesis of results › Pooled estimates of all-cause mortality after adjustment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Low-volume estimate as covariates are taken out, read from the figure (81 studies, 229 estimates): fully adjusted 0.97 (0.88-1.07); outliers removed 0.97 (0.89-1.05); abstainer biases removed 0.96 (0.87-1.06); Caucasian or not removed 0.95 (0.88-1.03); smoking status removed 0.91 (0.84-0.97); all covariates removed 0.86 (0.83-0.90). The abstainer-bias covariates moved the estimate little. The authors say an online appendix (not read) confirms former-drinker bias matters more than occasional-drinker bias.

anchors.extracted: Stratified models, adjusted for median age, sex and country. 13 studies against lifetime abstainers only: low volume 0.90 (0.76-1.06, p = .20; 50 estimates), occasional 0.94 (0.71-1.25; 4 estimates), former 1.31 (1.09-1.57). 41 studies with both biases: low volume 0.91 (0.83-1.00, p = .043). 24 with former-drinker bias only: 0.86 (0.78-0.95). 9 with occasional bias only: 0.86 (0.82-0.91). Figure 4 shows only the last two, the 13 and the 6 higher-quality studies (1.04).

anchors.locator: Table 5; Results › Synthesis of results › Meta-analysis of higher quality studies, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Method › Synthesis of results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Seven studies with lifetime abstainers only, an adequate intake measure, median age under 60 at intake and 55 or over at follow-up: low volume 0.89 (0.62-1.29; 39 estimates), former 1.14 (0.77-1.69). Friesema 2007 was influential (6 of its 8 estimates were extreme outliers). Without it (6 studies): low volume 1.04 (0.95-1.15; 35 estimates), former 1.31 (1.11-1.55), medium 1.29 (1.06-1.56). The studies are named only in an online appendix.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Summary of evidence, 5th and 9th paragraphs; Discussion › Conclusions, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Occasional drinkers had mortality risks similar to low-volume drinkers in every pooled model. Against occasional drinkers, low-volume drinkers would show no protection. The authors attribute the high former-drinker risk to people likely quitting for health reasons; this is an interpretation, not measured. They call the evidence on occasional-drinker bias mixed and unconfirmed.

Self-reported intake mostly under-reported; lifetime-abstainer classification can be unreliable; few studies in some stratified analyses; heavy episodic drinking could not be examined; findings concern net all-cause mortality only.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. One addition: Figure 3 prints its intermediate values, so they can be cited. Fully adjusted 0.97 (0.88-1.07); outliers removed 0.97 (0.89-1.05); abstainer biases removed 0.96 (0.87-1.06); Caucasian or not removed 0.95 (0.88-1.03); smoking status removed 0.91 (0.84-0.97); all covariates removed 0.86 (0.83-0.90). The abstainer-bias covariates moved the estimate least, and study-level smoking control moved it most. The caption does not say clearly whether covariates are removed one after another.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: Table 5 estimate counts sum to 87 and 77; the differences by row are 2, 4, 2, 2 and 0; the text says 8 estimates, 6 of them outliers.
Confirmed: Table 4 Model 1 rows sum to 178 (Table 1: 180); Model 3 rows sum to 69 (Table 1: 76); Models 2 and 4 match (140, 127).
Confirmed. A further typographical slip in the same table: 10 of 87 studies from Japan, China or India is printed as 11.47% (it is 11.49%).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low. Item 4 fails because the English-only restriction is not justified. Item 7 fails because the text mentions no list of excluded studies (the appendices are described as holding included studies, plots and covariates). Items 2 and 8 are rightly provisional.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's own list of gaps is accurate, but I would rate the gap 'substantial', not 'minor'. (1) The abstract concludes there is 'no net mortality benefit'. The adjusted intervals (0.88-1.07; 0.76-1.06 in bias-free studies) are compatible with 12 to 24% lower mortality, and only the post hoc 6-study model (1.04, 0.95-1.15) comes near excluding a benefit. (2) Discussion › Summary of evidence, 2nd paragraph, says the results fit a linear dose response better than a J-shape. The bias-free strata are not monotone: 13 studies 0.90, 0.95, 1.11, 1.42; 6 studies 1.04, 1.29, 1.07, 1.85. (3) Figure 4, offered as showing the estimate approaching 1 as biases are removed, leaves out the both-biases stratum (41 studies, 0.91). That stratum's point estimate is the same as the bias-free one (0.90). A judgment call for the senior author.

missed: Figure 3 prints its intermediate values (listed under key finding 5). Removing the abstainer-bias covariates changes the low-volume estimate only from 0.97 to 0.96. Removing study-level smoking control gives 0.91 (0.84-0.97). So in this meta-regression the move from 0.86 to 0.97 comes mostly from covariates other than how abstainers were defined.

Figure 4 (values printed): 24 studies with former-drinker bias 0.86 (0.78-0.95; 73 estimates), 9 with occasional-drinker bias 0.86 (0.82-0.91; 22), 13 bias-free 0.90 (0.76-1.06; 50), 6 higher-quality 1.04 (0.95-1.15; 35). It omits the 41 studies with both biases (0.91). The captions of Figures 3 and 4 say 'versus lifetime abstainers' although most strata shown used other reference groups.

Table 4 Model 1 (both biases, 0.91, 0.83-1.00) against Model 4 (bias-free, 0.90, 0.76-1.06): same point estimate, wider interval. This bears on any claim that the low-volume association shrinks as the reference group is defined more strictly.

Medium volume (25 to under 45 g a day) was significantly raised in the 6 higher-quality studies (1.29, 1.06-1.56). The 45 to under 65 g category was not significantly raised in any bias-free subset (1.11; 0.95; 1.07). Relevant to cl_alc_drinking_mortality_threshold.
